page_hint: Ch 3, §6 "An expert can be selected by noise stage"
quoted_clause: "Wan2.2 A14B is a useful counterexample to treating every mixture of experts as per-token top-k routing."
observed: A video-generation MoE case study (Wan2.2 noise-stage expert selection) sits inside Chapter 3's dense-vs-MoE discussion for language models. The architectural insight (not all MoE is per-token top-k) is valid, but the video-generation context is a second tangent in a chapter that already has a large alternative-inference tangent.
evidence: The section includes pinned GitHub revisions, function-level observations, and a figure (Fig 3.3). The reusable distinction (total weight storage vs active execution) is stated at the end, but could be made without the video-specific detail.
root_cause: A valid counterexample was expanded into a detailed case study in a chapter where the reader is focused on language-model parameter allocation.
correction: Compress to 1–2 sentences that state the counterexample ("not all MoE uses per-token top-k routing; some selection rules are timestep- or stage-dependent") and move the detailed Wan2.2 inspection to Ch 27 or an appendix. Preserve the citation.
acceptance_test: Ch 3 contains a brief counterexample note without implementation-level detail; the full inspection is in Ch 27 or an appendix with citation intact.

quoted_clause: "Assuming 'one token ≈ one word'" / "Ignoring the input–output asymmetry" / "Quoting context window as free capacity"
observed: Three of the five Common Mistakes in Ch 4 repeat mistakes already covered in Ch 1 (§5) and Ch 2 (§5): token≠word, input/output asymmetry, and context window as free capacity. The Ch 4 versions add the six-dimension framing but do not substantially deepen the earlier explanations.
evidence: Ch 1 §5 covers all three: "Assuming one token ≈ one word," "Ignoring the input/output asymmetry," and "Quoting context window as free capacity." Ch 2 §5 also covers input/output asymmetry. The Ch 4 versions restate the same points with minor contextual variation.
root_cause: Common Mistakes sections were populated per-chapter without checking for overlap with earlier chapters.
correction: Replace the three redundant items with mistakes specific to the six-dimension framework (e.g., "treating the six dimensions as independent when they interact," "sizing from one dimension while ignoring the binding constraint on another," "confusing declared traffic assumptions with derived occupancies"). Or condense the redundant items to one-line cross-references ("see Ch 1 §5").
acceptance_test: Ch 4's Common Mistakes section contains items that are specific to workload characterization and not already covered in Ch 1 or Ch 2.

quoted_clause: "That quadratic term is the single biggest reason context windows feel expensive"
observed: The claim that the quadratic attention term is "the single biggest reason context windows feel expensive" is stated without qualification. For decode, the KV cache memory (linear in context but large in absolute terms — ~335 GB at 128K for the canonical model) may be the more binding constraint. The sentence sits in the Attention subsection, where the quadratic term IS the dominant cost of the attention computation itself, but the phrase "context windows feel expensive" is broader than attention alone.
evidence: At 128K context: prefill attention is O(L²) position pairs (compute), while KV cache is ~335 GB (memory capacity). Which is "the single biggest reason" depends on whether the reader is thinking about compute cost or memory cost. The text does not specify the dimension.
root_cause: Overgeneralization from the attention-computation context to the broader context-window-cost context.
correction: Qualify the claim: e.g., "That quadratic term is the single biggest reason long-context *prefill compute* is expensive" or "one of the two biggest reasons context windows feel expensive (the other being KV-cache memory growth)."
acceptance_test: The claim specifies which dimension of cost it refers to (compute, memory, or both) and does not overstate the quadratic term's role in memory-constrained scenarios.

page_hint: Ch 2, §7 What We Still Don't Know (item 2)
quoted_clause: "Effect of continuous batching on the 2 × params × tokens approximation."
observed: The section title names continuous batching, but the content resolves the continuous-batching question (it does NOT reduce per-request FLOP count) and then pivots to prefix caching, where the actual open question (prefix-cache hit rate at fleet scale) is stated. The title does not match the unresolved content.
evidence: The text states: "it does not reduce the mathematical FLOP count per request" (resolved) and then: "The magnitude of the prefix-cache hit rate at fleet scale is not yet pinned down" (unresolved). The unresolved question is about prefix caching, not continuous batching.
root_cause: Section title was written for the first half of the content; the actual open question emerged in the second half.
correction: Rename to match the unresolved content, e.g., "Prefix-cache hit rate at fleet scale under realistic concurrency" — or split into two items: one stating the resolved continuous-batching conclusion (which belongs in the body, not in 'What We Don't Know') and one stating the prefix-cache open question.
acceptance_test: The section title accurately describes the unresolved question; resolved material is not listed under 'What We Still Don't Know.'

quoted_clause: "(~228 GB total resident with weights and workspace)"
observed: The 228 GB figure implies a ~64 GB runtime/workspace reserve (140 + 64 + 24.1 = 228.1), but the 64 GB reserve is never introduced or explained in Ch 2. It first appears in Ch 4's canonical workload box. A reader encountering 228 GB in Ch 2 cannot derive it from the information given in Ch 2.
evidence: Ch 2 states: weights 140 GB, KV 24.1 GB, total ~228 GB. 140 + 24.1 = 164.1, leaving ~64 GB unexplained. Ch 4 later states "~64 GB runtime/workspace [canonical scenario][ASSUMPTION] (the runtime/NCCL/activation reserve derived in Ch 7)."
root_cause: A value from Ch 4/Ch 7 is used in Ch 2 without introduction or cross-reference.
correction: Add a parenthetical in Ch 2: "(~228 GB total resident: 140 GB weights + ~64 GB runtime/workspace reserve + 24.1 GB KV — the reserve is introduced in Ch 4 and derived in Ch 7)" — or simply state the components.
acceptance_test: A reader in Ch 2 can derive 228 GB from the components stated in Ch 2, or is directed to where the missing component is introduced.

quoted_clause: "sizing for active parameters while forgetting the KV cache is dense"
observed: "The KV cache is dense" is ambiguous. It could mean (a) the KV cache is [as large as it would be for] a dense model [with the same attention shape] — the intended meaning, or (b) the KV cache uses dense (full-MHA) attention — which may not be true if the model uses GQA. Reading (b) would lead the reader to provision full-MHA KV for a GQA model.
evidence: The surrounding text discusses MoE vs dense parameter allocation, not attention architecture. The intended meaning is (a): MoE routing does not reduce KV cache size. But "the KV cache is dense" literally reads as a statement about attention architecture.
root_cause: Ambiguous compression of "the KV cache is [the same size as it would be for] a dense [model]" into "the KV cache is dense."
correction: Rephrase: "sizing for active parameters while forgetting that MoE routing does not reduce KV cache size" or "...while forgetting that the KV cache is provisioned from the attention shape, not the routing regime."
acceptance_test: The sentence cannot be misread as a claim about attention architecture (dense vs GQA).

page_hint: Ch 2, §7 What We Still Don't Know (item 3)
quoted_clause: "Cross-technology bandwidth numbers. ... [1P][FACT] — vendor-published specifications as of the 2026-08-30 cutoff; verify against the specific generation in use."
observed: Vendor bandwidth specifications (H200 4.8 TB/s, B200 ~8 TB/s, MI300X ~5.3 TB/s) are labeled [1P][FACT] — they are known facts, not open questions. Listing them under "What We Still Don't Know" conflates a caveat ("verify against your generation") with genuine uncertainty. The actual open question — how these compare to the 5.6 TB/s decode demand in a specific deployment — is workload-dependent and could be stated as such.
evidence: The bandwidth numbers are first-party specifications. The uncertainty is about applicability to a specific deployment, not about the numbers themselves. The section's own text says "vendor-published specifications" and "verify against the specific generation in use" — these are instructions, not open questions.

correction: Either move the bandwidth numbers to the body (as dated [1P][FACT] specifications with a verify caveat) and replace the 'What We Don't Know' entry with the actual open question ("which generation's bandwidth is available in our target deployment, and does it change the GPU count for the canonical decode demand?"), or reframe the entry to state the workload-dependent question rather than listing known specifications.
acceptance_test: Every item under 'What We Still Don't Know' states a question that is genuinely unresolved, not a known fact with a time-sensitivity caveat.

quoted_clause: FLOPs per embedding (64-token query)

page_hint: Ch 6, §1 metric hierarchy, final paragraph of Concept
quoted_clause: Diagnosis runs the other way

It could mean (a) opposite of the causal direction (serving → resource → workload) or (b) opposite of the listing order (resource → serving → workload). The intended meaning is (a), but the text has just discussed both the listing order and the causal direction, making the reference unclear.

quoted_clause: 40 × 1.29 ≈ 52 PFLOP/s ... ~18.6× oversubscribed
observed: The displayed intermediate (≈ 52 PFLOP/s) and the displayed result (~18.6×) are inconsistent at the displayed precision. 52 / 2.77 = 18.8, not 18.6. The result 18.6 comes from the more precise calculation 40 × 1.288 / 2.7692 = 18.60.
root_cause: Mixed precision: the intermediate is rounded to 2 significant figures (52) while the result uses 3 significant figures (18.6) from a more precise calculation.
correction: Either display the more precise intermediate: '40 × 1.288 ≈ 51.5 PFLOP/s ... ~18.6× oversubscribed' or round the result to match: '≈ 52 PFLOP/s ... ~18.8× oversubscribed.'
acceptance_test: A reader who computes displayed_intermediate / displayed_capacity gets the displayed_result within rounding tolerance.

quoted_clause: so goodput does not grow
observed: The initial claim 'goodput does not grow' is stated as a fact before the qualification that follows ('The unchanged claim holds only when...'). A reader who stops at the initial claim would form an incorrect general model.
evidence: The text states 'goodput does not grow' then immediately provides a counterexample where goodput rises (50×0.96=48 vs 70×0.94=65.8). The qualification comes after the claim.
root_cause: Claim stated before its scope condition, creating a window where the reader holds an overgeneralized model.
correction: Restructure: state the general principle first ('goodput = raw_rate × compliant_fraction; a throughput increase helps goodput only if the compliant fraction holds'), then give the specific example where it doesn't hold.
acceptance_test: The general principle is stated before the specific example, not after.

quoted_clause: the meaningful per-step data movement is a TP all-reduce of the per-layer activations (tens of MBs, not GBs, at the canonical batch and hidden size — it scales with batch × hidden width per layer)
observed: The parenthetical '(tens of MBs...)' is ambiguous: it could refer to each per-layer all-reduce or to the per-step total across all layers. For a 70B model with hidden_size ≈ 8192, batch 32, FP16, each per-layer activation all-reduce is ~512 KB (sub-MB), while the per-step total across ~80 layers is ~40 MB (tens of MBs). The phrase 'it scales with batch × hidden width per layer' suggests the per-step total, but the proximity to 'per-layer activations' invites the per-layer reading.
evidence: Per-layer activation for decode: batch × hidden_size × 2 bytes = 32 × 8192 × 2 = 524,288 bytes ≈ 512 KB. Per-step total across ~80 layers: 80 × 512 KB ≈ 40 MB. 'Tens of MBs' matches the per-step total, not the per-layer figure.
root_cause: Ambiguous referent for the quantity in parentheses.
correction: Rephrase to: 'the per-step total across all layers is tens of MBs (each individual per-layer all-reduce is sub-MB at the canonical batch and hidden size).'
acceptance_test: A reader should be able to determine from the sentence alone whether 'tens of MBs' refers to per-layer or per-step total.

quoted_clause: §1 first: 'These are not alternatives; production systems compose them (e.g. DP across nodes × TP within a node × PP across a few nodes…)' vs §1 second: 'The three primary patterns compose (e.g. DP across nodes × TP within a node × PP across a few nodes) — which dimension binds determines which to split first.'

evidence: Direct textual comparison within the same section.
root_cause: The figure prose paragraph restated a point already made before the figure.
correction: In the post-figure prose, keep only the new insight ('which dimension binds determines which to split first') and drop the repeated composition example, or merge the two into one occurrence.
acceptance_test: The composition point and its example appear once in §1; the post-figure prose adds only new content.

quoted_clause: 2 × 70 × 10⁹ × 8,000 ≈ 1.12 PFLOP — the book's K = 1,000, since 1,200 + 8,000 = 9,200; the full 9.2K canonical input is ~1.29 PFLOP
observed: The K = 1,000 house-convention reminder is embedded in the middle of a FLOP calculation, disrupting the arithmetic flow. The reader is following a numerical derivation and is interrupted by a definitional aside.
evidence: The reminder appears inline within the parenthetical of the FLOP calculation, between the 8K result and the 9.2K result.
root_cause: The convention reminder was placed at the point of use rather than in a footnote or at the start of the paragraph.
correction: Move the K = 1,000 reminder to a footnote or to the start of the paragraph (before the FLOP calculation), so the arithmetic flows uninterrupted.
acceptance_test: The FLOP calculation reads as a continuous derivation without an inline definitional interruption.

quoted_clause: 'the canonical 8×H100 host (640 GB total)' / 'the canonical host is 8×H100 and the canonical 70B has 80 layers' / 'the canonical 70B/8×H100 baseline uses intra-host TP=8'
observed: The canonical configuration (70B, 8×H100, 640 GB, 80 layers) is restated in full at multiple points within the chapter. Each restatement is individually correct, but the cumulative effect is mild redundancy.
evidence: At least three full restatements of the canonical configuration within Ch 10.

acceptance_test: The full canonical configuration (model size, GPU count, total HBM, layer count) is stated in full once; later references use a short form.

quoted_clause: the KV-cache footprint must fit the target host's aggregate memory
observed: "KV-cache" (hyphenated) appears as a compound modifier here, while "KV cache" (unhyphenated) is used throughout the rest of the chunk (e.g., Ch 11, Ch 12 §3, Ch 13, Ch 14).
evidence: Ch 12 §1: "KV-cache footprint"; Ch 12 §3: "KV cache for 9.2K context"; Ch 13: "KV for the 9.5K max context"; Ch 14: "KV cache utilization."
root_cause: Inconsistent hyphenation of a compound modifier.

acceptance_test: Global search for "KV-cache" returns only intentional compound-modifier uses, or zero if unhyphenated form is canonical.

quoted_clause: The KV-transfer arrow is the load-bearing cost — it moves the per-request KV state (~35 GB for the 13.3K-token context of §9.8; the canonical 9.2K-token request carries ~24.1 GB) across the joining link, so disaggregation pays only when the specialization benefit exceeds that transfer plus routing overhead. Caveat: see the in-figure aggregate-KV caveat (per-request times assume an unshared per-GPU link).
observed: The caption is very long (~80 words of dense numerical detail) and substantially duplicates Note 11.3-1, which appears immediately below the figure. Figure captions should orient the reader to what to look at; the detailed derivation belongs in the note/prose.
evidence: Caption contains ~35 GB, 13.3K tokens, 24.1 GB, 9.2K tokens, aggregate-KV caveat — all repeated in Note 11.3-1 with full derivation.

correction: Shorten the caption to the figure's purpose and key takeaway (e.g., "P/D disaggregation has two cases: within-NVLink and cross-host; the KV-transfer cost decides whether it pays — see Note 11.3-1 for derivation"). Move numerical detail to the note.
acceptance_test: Caption is under ~40 words and does not duplicate Note 11.3-1's numerical derivations.

quoted_clause: a single card sustains ~24,700 prefill tokens/s (989 TFLOP/s × 35% MFU ÷ 14 GFLOP/token = 24,725
observed: The same figure is written as "~24,700" in the prose and "24,725" in the parenthetical derivation. The rounding is inconsistent within the same sentence.

quoted_clause: KV cache / KV-cache
observed: Both 'KV cache' (two words) and 'KV-cache' (hyphenated) appear across the three chapters. E.g., Ch 15 §5: 'KV-cache blocks'; Ch 17 §3: 'KV cache management.'
evidence: String search across the chunk finds both spellings.

quoted_clause: illustratively FlashAttention‑class ~400 GB/s achieved vs naive SDPA ~150 GB/s achieved for 9,200‑token contexts
observed: FlashAttention is shown achieving HIGHER bandwidth (400 vs 150 GB/s) while the text argues it transfers FEWER bytes. A reader may find this counterintuitive without an explicit note that higher achieved bandwidth × shorter runtime = fewer total bytes.
evidence: The text's argument is correct (rate ≠ count), but the illustrative numbers show FlashAttention with higher bandwidth, which superficially contradicts 'fewer bytes' unless the reader understands that the kernel finishes faster.

quoted_clause: the same formula gives N_min = ceil(40 × 8.6 / 17) = 21 for the canonical peak, 22 with the reserve (case (ii))
observed: '22 with the reserve (case (ii))' conflates two different derivations of 22: (a) 21 KV-screen hosts + 1 N−1 reserve = 22, and (b) the case (ii) full-square prefill screen = 22 at zero spare. The parenthetical '(case (ii))' is ambiguous about which derivation is meant.
evidence: 21 + 1 = 22 (KV + reserve). ⌈21.81⌉ = 22 (case (ii) prefill, zero spare). Both give 22 but mean different things.
root_cause: Ambiguous parenthetical in figure caption.
correction: Disambiguate: e.g., '21 + 1 reserve = 22 (or 22 from the case (ii) prefill screen at zero spare — same number, different derivation).'
acceptance_test: The caption makes clear which derivation of 22 is intended, or notes that both coincide.

quoted_clause: Scope of the one-host framing (stated up front, matching Chapter 8's Scope note): the 8×H100 host here is the per-request feasibility container...

page_hint: Multi-step reasoning cost — β discussion vs W_reuse formula
quoted_clause: (to ~14.16 s / ~1.65× with 100% prefix reuse, a full increase of ~5.6 s)
observed: W_reuse(3) is stated as ≈ 14.14 s in the W formula section but as ~14.16 s in the β/task-multiplier discussion. The correct value from the stated inputs is 14.14 s: (11,600/9,200)×1.08 + 12.375 + 0.399 = 1.362 + 12.375 + 0.399 = 14.136 ≈ 14.14. The 14.16 s value is obtained by using 11,795 (the incorrect prefill count from AGT-01): (11,795/9,200)×1.08 + 12.375 + 0.399 = 14.159 ≈ 14.16. This also affects the stated multiplier: 14.14/8.58 = 1.648 ≈ 1.65× (correct with exact base 8.58), but 14.16/8.6 = 1.647 ≈ 1.65× (coincidentally also 1.65× with rounded base). The time value itself is inconsistent.
evidence: W_reuse(3) formula section states ≈ 14.14 s. Recomputing with 11,600 prefill tokens gives 14.136. Recomputing with 11,795 gives 14.159. The β section uses 14.16.
root_cause: Downstream consequence of AGT-01: the β discussion uses the incorrect 11,795 prefill count, producing 14.16 instead of 14.14.
correction: Change '~14.16 s' to '~14.14 s' in the β/task-multiplier discussion. Verify the multiplier: 14.14/8.58 = 1.648 ≈ 1.65× (keep 1.65× if using exact base 8.58; or change to 1.64× if using rounded base 8.6 — be consistent).
acceptance_test: W_reuse(3) is stated as 14.14 s in both locations, and the multiplier is consistent with the stated base (8.58 or 8.6).

quoted_clause: Every agentic request pays this at least once, and usually again for the intermediate reasoning the loop generates (the T·γ tokens).
observed: 'This' refers to L_base ≈ 8.6 s (1.08 s prefill + 7.5 s decode of 300 tokens). The intermediate reasoning is T×65 tokens, costing T×1.625 s of decode — far less than a full 8.6 s. A reader could conclude the full 8.6 s is paid twice (once for the final answer, once for intermediate reasoning), which would be incorrect. The intermediate reasoning adds decode time for γ tokens plus prefill of the grown prefix, not another full L_base.
evidence: L_base = 8.6 s for 300 output tokens. Intermediate reasoning = T×65 tokens × 25 ms = T×1.625 s. For T=3: 4.875 s of decode, not 8.6 s. The W formula correctly separates these components.
root_cause: Ambiguous pronoun 'this' — could refer to the specific 8.6 s value or the general concept of inference latency.
correction: Reword to: 'Every agentic request pays L_base at least once for the final answer, and pays additional decode time for the intermediate reasoning the loop generates (the T·γ tokens, ~1.6 s per turn at ~25 ms/token).' Or: '...pays this at least once, and pays additional inference time again for the intermediate reasoning...'
acceptance_test: A reader cannot reasonably conclude that the full 8.6 s L_base is paid twice for a T-turn request.

quoted_clause: the per-turn agent step averages ~120 ms ... λ_tool ≈ 100 ms (median, tool backend) ... So per-turn orchestration overhead L_agent ≈ 220 ms (median).
observed: λ_step is described as an 'average' (~120 ms) while λ_tool is described as a 'median' (~100 ms), but L_agent is claimed to be a 'median' (~220 ms). The sum of an average and a median is not necessarily a median (median(X+Y) ≠ median(X) + median(Y) in general). The text mixes statistical terms for components of the same sum.
evidence: 'averages ~120 ms' (average) + '~100 ms (median)' (median) = '~220 ms (median)' (claimed median). The sum of an average and a median does not yield a median without additional assumptions.
root_cause: Inconsistent statistical terminology across components of the same quantity.
correction: Either use 'average' for both components (giving an average L_agent ≈ 220 ms), use 'median' for both (if the 120 ms figure is also a median), or reword to 'L_agent ≈ 220 ms (typical/central estimate)' to avoid claiming a specific statistical measure.
acceptance_test: The statistical term (average, median, or approximate central tendency) is consistent across λ_step, λ_tool, and L_agent.

quoted_clause: the model's own per-turn work, prefill of the grown prefix + decode of γ, is carried inside W, ≈ 3.0–3.1 s marginal per turn
observed: The description says 'prefill + decode' (excluding tool), but the stated range 3.0–3.1 s matches the marginal cost INCLUDING the tool leg (2.94, 3.04, 3.14 s for turns 1–3). Prefill + decode only gives 2.80, 2.91, 3.01 s — a range of 2.8–3.0 s, not 3.0–3.1 s. Additionally, the range 3.0–3.1 does not cover turn 1's marginal cost (2.94 s with tool, 2.80 s without).
root_cause: The description ('prefill + decode') and the range (3.0–3.1) refer to different quantities — the range appears to include the tool leg while the description excludes it. Also, the range doesn't cover all turns.
correction: Either (a) change the description to 'prefill + decode + tool' and widen the range to '≈ 2.9–3.2 s' to cover turns 1–4, or (b) keep 'prefill + decode' and change the range to '≈ 2.8–3.0 s'. Specify which turns the range applies to if it doesn't cover all.
acceptance_test: The stated range matches the described components (prefill+decode or prefill+decode+tool) and covers the marginal costs for the turns it claims to describe.

quoted_clause: by Little's law (§2) vs Little's Law stays a mean relation (§8)
observed: The text uses both 'Little's law' (lowercase, §2) and 'Little's Law' (capitalized, §8) for the same concept.
evidence: §2: 'by Little's law'; §8: 'Little's Law stays a mean relation'.
root_cause: Inconsistent capitalization of the same proper noun.
correction: Standardize to one form throughout (either 'Little's law' or 'Little's Law').
acceptance_test: Text search confirms a single capitalization form for 'Little's' across the manuscript.

quoted_clause: ~2.0 req/s (§3) vs ~10 rps average (§2) vs 40 rps peak (§2)
observed: The text uses both 'req/s' and 'rps' for requests per second. 'rps' appears for arrival rates (10 rps, 40 rps); 'req/s' appears for capacity rates (~2.0 req/s).
evidence: §2: '~10 rps average and ~40 rps peak'; §3: '~2.0 req/s'; §8: '16 req/s'.
root_cause: Either an intentional distinction (arrival rate vs capacity rate) that is never stated, or an unintentional inconsistency.
correction: If intentional, state the convention explicitly (e.g., 'rps denotes arrival rate; req/s denotes capacity rate'). If unintentional, standardize to one form.

page_hint: Ch 20 §5 Common Mistakes, 'Overlooking data movement cost'
quoted_clause: the ~300 out-tokens are generated locally; only their egress crosses the network
observed: The parenthetical is confusing. Output tokens are generated on the GPU; they don't 'cross the network' during generation. The response is sent to the user, but this is trivially true for any response. The intended contrast (input retrieval requires network; output generation doesn't) is obscured.
evidence: The sentence contrasts input retrieval (network) with output generation (local), but 'only their egress crosses the network' implies the output tokens' network crossing is noteworthy, when the point is that output generation doesn't require network retrieval.
root_cause: Ambiguous phrasing that conflates 'response delivery to user' with 'network retrieval of input context.'
correction: Rewrite for clarity: 'the retrieved-context portion of the ~9,200 in-tokens must be fetched from a vector database or cache over the network, while the ~300 out-tokens are generated entirely on the host — only the final response needs to reach the user.'
acceptance_test: A reader can identify the network-cost asymmetry between input retrieval and output generation without re-reading.

quoted_clause: Fleet aggregate (8 hosts): 8 × (17/8.6) = 15.8 ≈ 16 req/s
observed: The mini-case gives the 8-host aggregate (16 rps) but not the 16-host aggregate, despite the question asking about scaling from 8 to 16 hosts.
evidence: The question asks 'what is the marginal cost per rps when scaling from 8 to 16 hosts?' The solution gives the 8-host aggregate and the per-host marginal cost but not the 16-host aggregate (16 × 1.977 = 31.6 ≈ 32 rps).
root_cause: The solution addresses the marginal cost (per-host rate) but doesn't explicitly state the target-fleet capacity.
correction: Add one sentence: 'At 16 hosts: 16 × (17/8.6) = 31.6 ≈ 32 req/s — still below the 40-rps peak, so 16 hosts would not meet peak demand.'
acceptance_test: The solution explicitly states the 16-host aggregate capacity.

quoted_clause: intelligent scheduling—such as consistent hashing for session affinity or predictive placement based on historical patterns—keeps utilization flat across the fleet and minimizes tail latency
observed: 'Keeps utilization flat' is a strong claim. In practice, utilization varies due to request heterogeneity, arrival patterns, and session-length variation. Intelligent scheduling reduces variance but doesn't eliminate it.
evidence: No evidence is provided for the claim that utilization is kept 'flat.' The Table 20-1 target of 'utilization variance < 0.2' acknowledges that variance exists.
root_cause: Overstated claim without qualification.
correction: Soften to 'tends to keep utilization more uniform across the fleet and reduces tail latency' or add a qualifier such as 'under stable arrival patterns.'
acceptance_test: The claim is consistent with the Table 20-1 utilization-variance target (which implies non-zero variance is expected).

quoted_clause: [canonical scenario] (Ch 4, Table 4-2)
observed: The label '[canonical scenario]' (lowercase, descriptive) is used instead of the house-convention label '[CANONICAL]' (uppercase, defined in Ch 4 and Appendix A).
evidence: House conventions define '[CANONICAL]' as the evidence-label vocabulary. Ch 21 §3 uses '[canonical scenario]'.
root_cause: Non-standard label formatting.
correction: Replace '[canonical scenario]' with '[CANONICAL]' to match the house-convention evidence-label vocabulary.
acceptance_test: Text search confirms '[CANONICAL]' is used consistently for canonical-scenario references.

page_hint: Ch 21 §7 What We Still Don't Know, item 2
quoted_clause: How well evaluation suites generalize across distribution shifts in real traffic is (to be verified)
observed: The phrase 'to be verified' is ambiguous: it could mean the manuscript hasn't done the research (illegitimate uncertainty) or that the property is genuinely uncertain and requires ongoing verification (legitimate).
evidence: The context ('a suite tuned on last quarter's data may misjudge this quarter's model') suggests genuine workload-dependent uncertainty, but the phrasing doesn't make this explicit.
root_cause: Ambiguous uncertainty label that doesn't distinguish 'unknown because evolving' from 'unknown because unresearched.'
correction: Clarify the uncertainty category: 'How well evaluation suites generalize across distribution shifts is workload-dependent and evolves with traffic patterns; no universal answer exists — this is an ongoing verification requirement, not a gap in this manuscript's research.'
acceptance_test: The uncertainty item clearly identifies which of the four legitimate categories (empirical data unavailable, workload-dependent, implementation-dependent, evolving) applies.

quoted_clause: The prefill/decode split is the figure the rest of the book builds on
observed: 'Figure' is used metaphorically to mean 'central concept' or 'distinguishing feature,' but the book uses 'figure' throughout to mean a numbered diagram (Fig 22.1, Fig 23.1, etc.). In a chapter that contains an actual figure, this metaphorical use could momentarily confuse a reader scanning for figure references.
evidence: The book's consistent usage: 'figure' = numbered diagram. This sentence uses 'figure' = concept/distinction.
root_cause: Metaphorical usage that collides with the book's technical terminology.
correction: Replace 'figure' with 'distinction,' 'concept,' or 'split': e.g., 'The prefill/decode split is the distinction the rest of the book builds on.'
acceptance_test: The word 'figure' in Ch 22 §2 refers only to numbered diagrams, not to concepts.

quoted_clause: The reasoning is traced by the architect working through the canonical loop as a structured investigation.
observed: Awkward sentence construction. 'Traced by the architect working through' is a dangling modifier / passive-voice construction that obscures the agent and action. The sentence's function (stating that the chapter demonstrates reasoning by walking through the loop) is clear but the phrasing is stilted.
evidence: Readability: the sentence requires re-reading to parse. 'Traced by' + gerund ('working through') creates an unclear grammatical structure.
root_cause: Overly compressed sentence that tries to state both what is demonstrated and who demonstrates it in one clause.
correction: Rewrite actively: 'The architect works through the canonical loop as a structured investigation, and the chapter traces that reasoning step by step.'
acceptance_test: The sentence parses on first read without re-reading.

quoted_clause: the regulated-data constraint (the dialogue does establish regulated data)
observed: The parenthetical '(the dialogue does establish regulated data)' reads as a defensive note to a reviewer rather than part of the narrative. It interrupts the flow of the bound statement. The dialogue does indeed establish regulated data (the Lead says 'It's internal and regulated'), so the parenthetical is accurate but stylistically out of place.
evidence: The Lead's line 'It's internal and regulated; keep it on-prem if at all possible' clearly establishes regulated data. The parenthetical is unnecessary for the reader.
root_cause: Likely a response to a prior review comment that was left in the text rather than resolved by removing the comment.
correction: Remove the parenthetical. The dialogue itself establishes regulated data; the reader can see this.
acceptance_test: Bound 5 states the constraint without a defensive parenthetical.

quoted_clause: with a 200-rps burst buffer (an arrival-rate buffer: bursts of duration D queue and drain at the measured per-host rate r (≤141 rps at 100% MFU, ~42–57 at 30–40%); max queue wait ≈ D·(200−r)/r must stay inside the 3 s SLO — so state D, the buffer depth D·(200−r) requests, and either add capacity, add admission control, or scope the SLO to non-burst traffic; worked: D = 1 s at 200 rps → queue depth 200 × 1 = 200 requests, drained at ~50 rps in ~4 s — burst-window requests miss the 3 s SLO, so the burst runs under a separate queue-and-drain degraded-mode SLO (option a))
observed: The entire burst-buffer explanation — formula, assumptions, worked example, conclusion, and architectural response — is embedded in a single parenthetical within one already-long sentence. The sentence contains three levels of nested parentheses and a semicolon-separated sequence of five clauses. This is extremely difficult to parse and is the kind of passage where a reader is likely to skip the parenthetical entirely, missing the queueing reasoning that is the mini-case's key architectural insight.
evidence: The parenthetical is approximately 100 words with nested parentheses, semicolons, em-dashes, and a worked example — all inside one sentence's parenthetical.
root_cause: The author compressed a multi-step queueing argument into a parenthetical to avoid breaking the mini-case's narrative flow, but the compression makes the content unreadable.
correction: Extract the burst-buffer explanation from the parenthetical into a separate sentence or short paragraph after the main mini-case sentence. The main sentence can state the conclusion ('with a burst buffer that queues and drains under a degraded-mode SLO'), and the following sentence/paragraph can present the formula, worked example, and reasoning.
acceptance_test: The burst-buffer formula, worked example, and conclusion are readable without nested parentheses exceeding one level.

quoted_clause: total prefill compute becomes increasingly dominated by the quadratic attention term as context grows (including the 9.2K canonical case)
observed: The parenthetical '(including the 9.2K canonical case)' is ambiguous. It could be read as 'the trend toward quadratic dominance includes 9.2K' (correct: 9.2K is on the trajectory) or 'at 9.2K the quadratic term already dominates' (incorrect: it is 17% of the linear term under full-square, 8.6% under causal-triangle). The next sentence clarifies that 9.2K is 'still subordinate,' but the parenthetical alone permits the wrong reading.
evidence: At 9.2K, quadratic/linear = 17% (full-square) or 8.6% (causal-triangle). The quadratic term does not dominate at 9.2K.
root_cause: Compressed parenthetical that doesn't distinguish 'on the trajectory toward' from 'already at.'
correction: Rewrite as '(a trend that includes the 9.2K canonical case, where the quadratic term is still subordinate — see ratios below)' or simply remove the parenthetical since the ratios immediately following make the point.
acceptance_test: A reader cannot interpret the parenthetical as claiming quadratic dominance at 9.2K.

page_hint: Ch 24 §8 mini-case, opening paragraph; Table 24-1 Cycle 2
quoted_clause: the poisoned‑hit rate sits exactly at its ≈0.003 ceiling
observed: The §4.1 target is '< 0.003' (strict inequality). The Cycle 2 value is 0.003. Under strict inequality, 0.003 does not meet < 0.003. The text identifies 'two metrics remain above target' (FP rate and guardrail-trigger rate) and then mentions the poisoned-hit rate separately as sitting 'exactly at its ceiling,' leaving ambiguous whether it meets the target. With a strict-inequality target, being exactly at 0.003 means not meeting it — which would make three metrics at-or-above target, not two.
evidence: §4.1 table: target '< 0.003 (0.003 per query)'. Table 24-1 Cycle 2: 0.003. 0.003 is not < 0.003.
root_cause: Boundary case with a strict inequality target and a value exactly at the threshold; the text handles it with ≈ and 'ceiling' language but does not explicitly state whether the metric passes.
correction: Either change the target to '≤ 0.003' in §4.1, or explicitly state in the mini-case that the poisoned-hit rate is at-but-not-below the target (making it a third metric requiring attention), or clarify that ≈0.003 means slightly below 0.003.
acceptance_test: Confirm that the mini-case's count of 'two metrics above target' is consistent with the §4.1 target definitions under strict inequality, or that the target has been relaxed to ≤.

quoted_clause: We define the *prompt-injection exposure surface* (PIES) as an **illustrative local attack-surface count**: the number of distinct prompt-pattern classes an adversary can successfully submit through all user‑facing entry points
observed: The initial definition says PIES = classes an adversary can 'successfully submit.' Later in the same section, PIES is redefined as 'the subset of those candidate classes with ≥1 guardrail bypass in the cycle,' and CPS (= 217) is introduced as the full candidate pattern space. If 'successfully submit' means 'the entry point accepts the input,' then the initial definition matches CPS, not PIES. If it means 'the attack bypasses guardrails,' it matches the later PIES definition. The ambiguity is that the same term 'exposure surface' is used for both the initial PIES definition and, implicitly, for CPS when the text calls CPS 'the unique exposure surface.'
evidence: Initial: PIES = 'classes an adversary can successfully submit.' Later: 'the unique exposure surface is the candidate pattern space, CPS = 217' and 'PIES is the subset of those candidate classes with ≥1 guardrail bypass.' §4.1 table: PIES = 'Subset of the candidate pattern space (CPS) with ≥1 guardrail bypass.' The initial definition and the §4.1 definition use different criteria unless 'successfully submit' is read as 'successfully bypass.'
root_cause: The word 'successfully' is doing unexplained work — it must mean 'bypasses guardrails' for the definitions to agree, but this is not stated. Additionally, 'exposure surface' is used for both the initial PIES concept and for CPS.
correction: Clarify the initial definition: either 'successfully submit AND bypass guardrails' or restructure to introduce CPS first (all submittable classes) and then define PIES as the bypass subset. Avoid using 'exposure surface' for both CPS and PIES without distinguishing them.
acceptance_test: Read the initial PIES definition and the §4.1 table definition side by side; confirm they use the same criterion without requiring the reader to infer that 'successfully submit' means 'bypasses.'

quoted_clause: Column header "FACT Target" vs cost row cell "DERIVED from FACT inputs, §26.8 — not itself a FACT"
observed: The column is titled "FACT Target" but the cost row explicitly states the value is "not itself a FACT." This creates a labeling tension: the column header implies FACT status, while the cell negates it. The other three rows (SM util < 80%, hit ratio > 30%, fallback rate < 10%) are targets/thresholds, not FACTs either — they are criteria to be verified. The column name is ambiguous about whether "FACT" modifies "Target" (a target stated as a fact about requirements) or implies the values are FACTs.
evidence: Column header: "FACT Target." Cost cell: "not itself a FACT." The other cells are thresholds ("< 80%", "> 30%", "< 10%") which are targets, not measurements. No row in the column contains an actual FACT (measured runtime quantity).
root_cause: The column header was likely intended to mean "target that will be verified as FACT" or "target stated with FACT-level precision," but the cost row's explicit disclaimer exposes the ambiguity.
correction: Rename the column to something unambiguous, e.g., "Verification target" or "Acceptance threshold," and move the FACT/DERIVED provenance note to a column footnote or the row's own provenance label. Alternatively, add a brief header footnote explaining what "FACT Target" means.
acceptance_test: A reader can determine from the column header alone whether the values are FACTs, targets to be verified, or derived quantities, without needing to read individual cell disclaimers.

quoted_clause: "[1P] arXiv:2606.19348; arXiv:2607.24653; HF Qwen/Qwen3.8-Flash-Next; HF zai-org/GLM-5.3-Flash]"
observed: The caption ends with a closing square bracket "]" that has no matching opening bracket. The preceding "[1P]" has its own matched brackets. The sources list appears to be missing an opening "[" or the trailing "]" is stray.

acceptance_test: All square brackets in the Fig A.1 caption are matched.

quoted_clause: "~2.0 rps" (Step 2) vs "~2.0 req/s per-host ceiling" (Table 26-3, Pattern A row)
observed: The same unit (requests per second) is abbreviated as "rps" in Step 2 and "req/s" in Table 26-3. Both appear within the same chapter.
evidence: Step 2: "from ~2.0 rps to ~1.3 rps." Table 26-3: "past the ~2.0 req/s per-host ceiling." Same quantity, same chapter, two abbreviations.
root_cause: Inconsistent unit abbreviation across sections of the same chapter.
correction: Standardize on one abbreviation (either "rps" or "req/s") throughout the chapter. Check the rest of the book for the same inconsistency.
acceptance_test: A global search for both abbreviations returns results from only one convention (or the book explicitly notes both are acceptable).

quoted_clause: "prefill-queue inflation at ρ near 1"
observed: The claim that ρ is "near 1" is not obviously supported by the numbers in this chunk. If the queue-drained service time is 120 + 80 + 50 = 250 ms and the uncached arrival rate is 2.0 rps, then ρ = 2.0 × 0.250 = 0.50, which is not "near 1." If the service time is taken as the inflated 450 ms, then ρ = 2.0 × 0.450 = 0.90, but using a queue-inflated response time to compute ρ is circular. The 200 ms queue inflation (320 − 120) also seems small for ρ truly near 1 under standard queueing models. Step 1 (not in this chunk) may contain the derivation that resolves this.
evidence: ρ = λ × S. With λ = 2.0 rps and S = 250 ms (queue-drained service time): ρ = 0.50. With S = 450 ms (including inflation): ρ = 0.90 but this is circular. The 200 ms inflation at ρ = 0.50 would be unexpected under M/M/1 (predicted Wq ≈ 250 ms at ρ = 0.50 with S = 250 ms), though continuous-batching dynamics differ from M/M/1. The text does not specify which queue or resource ρ refers to.
root_cause: The ρ claim may be derived in Step 1 with details not visible in this chunk, or it may be a qualitative approximation that does not match the chunk's own numbers.
correction: Verify against Step 1. If Step 1 derives ρ, ensure the value is consistent with "near 1" and with the 200 ms inflation. If ρ refers to a specific sub-queue (e.g., prefill queue utilization) rather than overall system utilization, state this explicitly. If the numbers do not support "near 1," replace with the actual ρ or a more accurate qualitative description (e.g., "at high utilization").
acceptance_test: The stated ρ value (or qualitative description) is consistent with the arrival rate and service time given in Step 1/Step 2, and the queue inflation magnitude is consistent with the stated ρ under the system's queueing model.

quoted_clause: "Each entry is a pattern template with eight fields: name, problem solved, triggering symptom, mechanism, minimal FACT set, trade-off, conditions of failure, and chapter pointer."
observed: The text states eight fields, but Table 26-3 has seven columns because "problem solved" and "triggering symptom" are combined into a single column titled "Problem solved (triggering symptom)." A reader counting columns will find seven, not eight.
evidence: Table 26-3 columns: Pattern | Problem solved (triggering symptom) | Mechanism | Minimal FACT set | Trade-off | Conditions of failure | Pointer = 7 columns. Text says 8 fields.
root_cause: The prose enumerates the conceptual fields while the table merges two fields into one column for space reasons, without noting the merge.
correction: Either (a) change "eight fields" to "seven table columns covering eight fields (problem solved and triggering symptom share a column)," or (b) split the combined column into two, or (c) reword to "each entry covers: name, problem, trigger, mechanism, ..." without claiming a specific field count that must match column count.
acceptance_test: The stated field count in the prose is reconcilable with the table's column count, either by matching or by an explicit note explaining the merge.

issue: The left-column token labels denote the step in which each token is SAMPLED, but the arrows feed directly into the 'append K/V' box with no visual indication of the one-step delay before the K/V is written. Read standalone, 'token2 / first decode → append K/V' implies token2's K/V is appended during the first decode step, which contradicts the book's own timing convention (printed p. 14: a token's K/V enters the cache on the step in which it is input, one step after it is sampled). The caption states the offset correctly, so the figure+caption unit is not wrong — but the diagram alone invites the exact misreading the book later devotes a paragraph to correcting.
evidence: Drawn labels: 'token1 / from prefill', 'token2 / first decode', 'token3 / second decode', '… tokenn / nth decode', each with an arrow into 'append K/V per layer·head'. Caption: 'written when that token is next processed as input, one step after it is sampled.' Under the book's convention, token1 (sampled at end of prefill) has its K/V written in the first decode step, and token2 (sampled in first decode) in the second decode step — i.e., every arrow crosses a step boundary that the figure does not mark.
acceptance_test: Either relabel the boxes to name the write step (e.g., 'token1 — appended in first decode') or add a short annotation on the arrow group such as 'appended one step later, when the token becomes input', so the drawn timing matches the caption without requiring the caption to rescue the diagram.

issue: Caption says the pipeline is shown 'in three bands' but only ever names two of them (PREFILL top, DECODE bottom); the third band is never identified. The subsequent sentence — 'The three bands and the single PERSISTENT KV CACHE box are conceptual groupings' — then counts the KV cache box separately from the three bands, leaving the band inventory ambiguous. Visually the page shows two outlined band containers (prefill row, decode row) plus the standalone cache box, so a reader cannot reconcile 'three bands' with what is drawn or with the caption's own enumeration.
evidence: Caption, sentence 1: 'The canonical end-to-end inference pipeline, in three bands. PREFILL (top) is … DECODE (bottom) is …' (no middle band named). Caption, later: 'The three bands and the single PERSISTENT KV CACHE box are conceptual groupings for teaching, not runtime components.' Rendered figure: light rounded containers enclose only the PREFILL row and the DECODE row; the PERSISTENT KV CACHE box is a separate element between them.
acceptance_test: Caption names all three bands explicitly (e.g., 'PREFILL (top), cache-I/O (middle), DECODE (bottom)') and the band/cache sentence no longer double-counts or omits an element — or the caption is restated as 'two processing bands plus the persistent KV cache' if only two bands are intended.

figure: Figure 3.4 (Dense vs MoE parameter allocation and KV cache behavior)
issue: Possible missing word-space (and possibly missing 'B' unit suffix) in the dense-column annotation. At 150 dpi the body line renders as 'every token activates all70B params' with no visible space between 'all' and '70B', and the caption line appears to read 'A dense 70B activates all 70 parameters per token', where the 'B' suffix may be absent. Cannot be resolved at this resolution — flagged for verification, not asserted as a confirmed defect.
evidence: Rendered page, dense column, second annotation line under the blue swatch: 'every token activates all70B params' (compare adjacent lines where spaces render clearly, e.g., 'KV grows linearly with context'). Caption, Parameter-activation contrast sentence: 'A dense 70B activates all 70 parameters per token (resident weights ≈ 140 GB ...)'. If the caption truly lacks 'B', it states 70 parameters rather than 70B parameters, which is semantically wrong; if only the space is missing in the body label, it is a typesetting nit. All other Figure 3.4 arithmetic independently re-derived and consistent (8 × 11.4 = 91.2 ≈ 91 GB; 6 × 11.4 = 68.4 ≈ 68; 2 × 11.4 = 22.8 ≈ 23; 91 + 3 ≈ 94 GB; 11.4B + 1.4B = 12.8B × 2 B = 25.6 GB; 1.31 MB/token × 9.2K ≈ 12 GB; 0.0655 MB/token × 9.2K ≈ 0.6 GB; 12.8/47 ≈ 27%).
root_cause: Unresolved at 150 dpi: either a missing interword space in the figure source, a missing 'B' in the caption source, or benign tight kerning.
correction: If verification confirms the defects: insert the word space in the body label ('all 70B params') and restore the unit suffix in the caption ('all 70B parameters'). If verification shows both are present, close as false positive.
acceptance_test: Re-render Figure 3.4 at ≥300 dpi (or inspect the figure source) and confirm: (a) body annotation reads 'all 70B params' with a word space; (b) caption reads 'activates all 70B parameters per token'. Both must be confirmed present; otherwise apply the correction.

figure: Figure 26.1 — Workload fingerprints on the six axes
issue: The in-figure title contains editorial meta-commentary — '(grouped bars, not radar)' — that is meaningless to a first-time reader, and the title otherwise near-duplicates the caption verbatim.
evidence: In-figure title: 'Workload fingerprints on six axes (grouped bars, not radar)'. Caption: 'FIGURE 26.1: Workload fingerprints on the six axes.' The word 'radar' appears nowhere in the visible text of pp. 424–425 (the provenance note on PDF 424 / printed 404 discusses axes and authored 0–1 scores but never mentions a radar chart), so the parenthetical reads as a note to a designer/reviewer that survived into the built PDF rather than reader-facing content.

acceptance_test: Grep the built PDF for 'not radar' and 'radar': zero hits outside any deliberate prose discussion; the figure title and caption no longer repeat the same phrase, and the legend note 'per-axis 0-1 scale; compare within an axis, not across axes' remains the sole statement of the comparison rule.

figure: Figure 25.1 — The Anatomy of an Architecture Decision Record
issue: The supersession arrow is drawn from the bottom of the ADR-001 field stack (below the Alternatives box) rather than from the Consequences box it names, and the figure label asserts a relation the caption hedges.

The figure's whole point is the consequences→context handoff, so the drawn anchor is the semantic payload of the diagram.

issue: Caption ends with a deictic cross-reference that resolves to nothing on the printed page: 'See the paragraph below for the Fig 7.1 link and the re-derivation caveat.' The full rendered page shows the figure and caption occupying the upper portion, with blank space to the page bottom — no paragraph appears below the caption on this page.
evidence: Full-page 150 dpi render of PDF p.448 inspected end to end; last content on the page is the Figure A.2 caption; the remainder of the page is empty. The paragraph containing the promised Fig 7.1 link and re-derivation caveat is not at the stated location (it was not located within this batch, which contains only pp. 448, 451, 452, 459).

If it is not immediately below the Figure A.2 caption on p.448, replace 'below' with an explicit, verifiable pointer (e.g., 'in §A.x, following this section' or 'see the paragraph introducing Fig 7.1'); rebuild and confirm the named location actually contains that paragraph.
